title: With desire I have desired (Luke 22:14–23)
hook: he longed to eat this Passover with them, and gives bread and cup
tomorrow: I am among you as one who serves

segments.voice: Yesterday, an upper room, furnished and waiting. Your line was make ready.

The room is ready. The hour has come. And Luke slows down. Before the bread, before the cup, before any of the words churches still repeat, Jesus says something personal. A dinner with someone not seen in years, a holiday table after a long time away: there's a kind of wanting that arrives before the food does. Jesus sits down with the twelve, and the first thing he tells them is how much he has wanted this evening.

In the King James words: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer." Some readers hear in that doubling a Hebrew way of speaking carried into Greek: very much, with all of me. I have longed and longed. He knows what's coming, and wants to be at this table anyway. Then something that can surprise a first-time reader: Luke has two cups. First Jesus takes a cup, gives thanks, and tells them to share it. Then he takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it, and gives it to them: "This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me." After supper, another cup: "This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you." Jewish tradition describes several cups through the Passover meal, though no one can say exactly how it ran in Jesus' day. Remembrance, in Greek, is anamnesis. Some Christians hear more than memory in it: the past brought into the present. Christians understand the meal in different ways, and it's fair to say each plainly. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ. Lutherans and many Anglicans speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine. Many other Protestants keep the meal as a holy memorial and a sign. Each of them keeps it, because he asked. And then the hard line: the hand of the one who betrays him is on the table. They start asking each other who it could be.
screen: then, large: `WITH DESIRE I HAVE DESIRED.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've been meaning to eat with and haven't, too busy, too far, too awkward, and picture the table: what you'd serve, where they'd sit. Imagine telling them at the start, before the food, that you've been looking forward to this; not a speech, just the truth. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.
Anamnesis, Greek for remembrance, do this in remembrance of me: a memory some hear as the past brought into the present.
Your line: I have longed for this. He said it first, before the bread. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians keep the Lord's Supper, also called Communion, the Eucharist or the Divine Liturgy, in weekly or even daily worship in some churches and monthly or quarterly in others, repeating Jesus's words over the bread and cup.

original.note: Greek: with desire I desired. a doubled phrase in the Hebrew manner, meaning intense longing.

what a scholar hears: the doubled 'desire desired' is read as a Semitic intensifier, and Luke, unlike Matthew and Mark, has a cup before the bread as well as the cup after supper.

notes: Luke 22:19b–20 is absent from a few Western manuscripts (notably Codex Bezae); most modern editions include it. Mentioned only in the trapdoor. Confirm.
Four cups at Passover are attested in the Mishnah (Pesachim 10), which is later than Jesus; the script says 'several cups' and that nobody knows exactly how the meal ran then. Confirm.
Communion views summarized: Catholic and Orthodox (change into body and blood), Lutheran and many Anglican (real presence), many other Protestants (memorial and sign). Confirm each is fairly stated.
'Desire desired' as a Semitic intensifier (cognate dative): standard commentary. Confirm.
